To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
price discrimination may intensify price competition and that the resulting price and welfare effects are ambiguous.
price discrimination in oligopoly may intensify price competition and lead to lower prices for consumers; and that the firms' profits are not necessarily reduced by the escalation of competition.

price discrimination by an oligopoly may lead to higher prices for some consumer groups, lower prices for others, and higher profits for all firms; price discrimination may be welfare improving for all consumer groups; firms may be worse off under discriminatory pricing; and firms may benefit from unilateral commitments not to engage in price discrimination.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (i) how the intensity of price competition is affected by price discrimination; (ii) how price discrimination affects the welfare of different consumer groups; and (iii) how firms can commit themselves not to engage in price discrimination.
the strategic implications of price discrimination in imperfectly competitive markets.
the strategic interaction between price discrimination and price competition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

third degree price discrimination is an important phenomenon that can be a source of significant welfare gains, but that the potential welfare gains are not always realized and the gains are not always shared by consumers.
price discrimination is not necessarily a bad thing for the economy.
third-degree price discrimination may intensify price competition and lead to lower prices for some consumers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
price discrimination may be a source of competitive advantage for firms that can credibly commit to it.
firms may wish to commit to price discrimination, and that the welfare consequences of such commitments are ambiguous.
price discrimination may be an equilibrium outcome, but that the equilibrium may not be stable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of price discrimination on consumer welfare depend on market structure and that firms can influence these effects by strategic commitments.
price discrimination by imperfectly competing firms can have very different effects on competition and welfare than the textbook case of price discrimination by a monopolist.
the effects of discrimination on firm and consumer welfare depend on the nature of the competition between firms, which may in turn be affected by their commitment to discriminate.
